transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-01-29 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SA), Maya Thompson (Head of ML, Zenith), Luis Ortega (VP Eng), Hannah Park (Finance), Derek Smith (SRE)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Zenith's budget constraints for an LLM-assisted payments product, tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem), and immediate levers (batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization) to hit per-token targets. Customer is cost sensitive due to regulatory reserve and is also latency-conscious on fraud workflow. They want a small pilot to validate unit economics before exec approval.

Topics Covered:
- Current stack and traffic profile
- Target per-inference cost / budget ceiling
- Latency SLOs for fraud vs analytics
- Data residency and SOC2/KMS needs
- Batching/caching levers and expected savings
- Pilot scope, benchmarks and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for jumping on, um, I'll kick off real quick — Redwood here, I'm Alex, AE, with Priya and Jordan from the engineering side.
[00:12] Luis Ortega: Hey thanks, Luis here. We grabbed Hannah and Maya; Derek just hopped on. We're tight on budget, so sorry in advance if we pepper you with questions.
[00:20] Maya Thompson: Yeah, quick note — our core use case is fraud triage messages and a customer support generation pipeline. The fraud path needs sub-200ms for the first token ideally, it's kind of a hard SLO.
[00:32] Priya Nair: Got it. Sub-200 for first token is tight, we can talk through hosting options that favor latency — Dedicated or private with edge placement — and tradeoffs for unit cost.
[00:45] Hannah Park: To be clear from finance: we have a per-customer monthly budget cap allocated for this feature. I'd like to understand a worst-case per-token number, and what levers we can pull to keep it under that.
[00:55] Jordan Lee: Also want to call out caching — prefix / KV caching often gives the biggest delta for repeated prompts. If your fraud flows reuse contexts, savings can be 30–60% in token cost in practice.
[01:10] Derek Smith: Quick infra note: we can't do air-gapped on day 1 — we need VPC peering with our AWS account and KMS integration for keys. SOC2 is a must.
[01:22] Alex Chen: That's fine, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we have SOC2 docs; I'll share the link. For the budget question, maybe can you share target per-transaction cost?
[01:32] Hannah Park: We eyeballed $0.003 per inference as the high watermark, that would be the max product can sustain.
[01:40] Priya Nair: Ok, that helps. Roughly speaking — hosted can be easiest to start, but per-token will be higher than dedicated. With batching and caching, Hosted can approach your number for async analytics, but fraud SLOs pushing <200ms for first token likely push you to Dedicated or Private.
[01:55] Maya Thompson: Can you give an example? Like, for a 1k-token response what's the delta between hosted and dedicated?
[02:04] Priya Nair: Sure — approximate numbers only: On hosted (managed multi-tenant) for a 1k token response, you're looking at say $0.15–0.25 per call depending on model. On Dedicated with reserved capacity and optimized quantized runtime maybe $0.06–0.10 per call. But that's heavily dependent on batching and concurrent throughput.
[02:25] Luis Ortega: Those ranges are big. How much of that comes from the model choice vs runtime levers?
[02:31] Jordan Lee: Split is roughly: model compute and token count are the base, then serving levers (batching, sequence-length-aware kernels, KV cache hit rate) can knock 2–4x off cost for common patterns. So if you have a 40% cache hit and good batching you compress that $0.15 down substantially.
[02:48] Hannah Park: What about the fixed commitment for Dedicated? Finance needs an idea of minimum monthly spend if we go dedicated.
[02:54] Alex Chen: Typical Dedicated starts at a monthly reserved capacity equivalent to X GPUs, which for a small pilot might be in the $20k–$40k/mo range depending on GPU type and model. We can do a small reserved pool and autoscaling for bursts.
[03:10] Maya Thompson: Hmm, that's higher than we were hoping. Is there a hybrid — start hosted and move to dedicated once volumes justify?
[03:17] Priya Nair: Absolutely — a lot of customers start on Hosted to validate prompts and quality, then transition to Dedicated for predictable unit economics. Redwood supports pinning model versions so behavior stays consistent across that transition.
[03:29] Derek Smith: For VPC peering — what's the network egress cost profile? If we run Private with peered traffic do we avoid major egress charges?
[03:38] Jordan Lee: With Private in your VPC we don't egress through public internet, so it's within your cloud's internal network costs; you'll see normal AWS cross-AZ or cross-region charges, but not our public egress fees. We'll provide a breakdown.
[03:50] [05:00] Maya Thompson: Sorry jump ahead — can you explain how prefix caching would work for us? We have many similar transaction contexts.
[05:09] Priya Nair: Sure. Prefix (or KV) caching stores previously computed transformer KV states for repeated prefixes. If your fraud flow reuses the same prompt header — you can bypass re-computing first N tokens. Practically, we see 20–60% token and compute savings depending on repetition. It also reduces latency because fewer tokens are recomputed.
[05:31] Luis Ortega: That sounds promising. What's the catch? Consistency? Staleness?
[05:36] Priya Nair: Good point — if the prompt includes dynamic customer data you need to control the cache key granularity to avoid leaking or serving stale info. Redwood supports scoping caches per-customer and TTLs.
[05:48] Hannah Park: On the security side, we need audit logs tied to keys and retention for 7 years for compliance. Is that supported?
[05:55] Alex Chen: We have audit logging in the Console with configurable retention — long-term archiving is an add-on, we can include that in the enterprise package and show estimated costs.
[06:04] Maya Thompson: Another quick question — quantization: how much accuracy loss should we expect, especially for generation quality in customer support flows?
[06:12] Priya Nair: For certain 8-bit and 4-bit quantization profiles we've seen negligible quality degradation on many open LLMs for generation tasks — but it depends on the model and your prompt set. We'll run evals as part of the pilot.
[06:24] [08:00] Hannah Park: About pilot scope — we want a 4-week pilot that demonstrates hitting $0.003 per inference in the analytics path and shows tradeoffs for fraud. What would Redwood need to run that?
[08:12] Alex Chen: We'll need sample prompts (top 10), token length distribution, desired concurrency and SLOs, and a target dataset for evals. Priya will sketch a benchmark plan. We'll also supply a sample cost model spreadsheet.
[08:25] Maya Thompson: For the fraud path, if we can't hit <200ms on Hosted, can dedicated get us below that?
[08:33] Priya Nair: Yes — Dedicated with colocated endpoints and pre-warmed KV cache can get sub-200ms for first token, depending on model and sequence lengths. The tradeoff is the reserved cost.
[08:44] Derek Smith: How much does batching hurt tail latency? If we batch aggressively for cost, do we risk missing SLOs?
[08:50] Jordan Lee: There's a tradeoff. Continuous batching improves throughput but can add queuing latency. Redwood supports workload-aware batching that respects per-route latency targets; you can set priority for fraud routes to bypass batching or use smaller micro-batches.
[09:02] Luis Ortega: Can you quantify savings from batching on a dataset like ours — mostly short queries (200–400 tokens) with occasional long-form support generation?
[09:12] Priya Nair: For short queries, batching often yields modest per-token savings (20–50%) depending on concurrency. For the long-form ones batching is more effective since amortized overhead per request is lower. Exact numbers we'll provide after the benchmark.
[09:25] [12:00] Hannah Park: I want to understand total cost of ownership — so far I'm hearing hosted has lower up-front but higher per-token, dedicated higher up-front lower per-token, private adds more ops but helps with compliance. What other hidden costs should we consider?
[12:14] Alex Chen: Operational costs: model updates, monitoring and eval maintenance, storage for cache and logs, and potential costs for high-retention observability. Also, commitment penalties if you underutilize reserved capacity. We can model utilization scenarios.
[12:35] Maya Thompson: Another question — we use a proprietary model variant internally. Can Redwood serve customer-supplied models in Private?
[12:42] Jordan Lee: Yes, in Private deployments you can bring-your-own-model; we help with onboarding. For Dedicated we currently support a set of verified models but can discuss custom onboarding if committed.
[12:55] Derek Smith: Any mention of encryption at rest and key rotation?
[13:00] Alex Chen: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS for key rotation policies and at-rest encryption. We'll send the security pack.
[13:08] [15:00] Maya Thompson: Ok, that's helpful. Let's talk numbers for a micro-pilot: if we do a 4-week pilot on Hosted with targeted batching and cache config, what's the estimated spend?
[15:17] Priya Nair: For a pilot with modest volumes — assume 50k requests/day with average 300 tokens — with caching reducing effective tokens by 30%, you might land in the $4k–$8k range for the month on Hosted. That includes monitoring and standard retention.
[15:30] Hannah Park: That's within our pilot budget. The concern is the production run — if we scale to 1M requests/day we need better unit economics.
[15:39] Alex Chen: Right — that's where Dedicated or Private with reserved capacity and quantization profiles becomes compelling. We can model the break-even point in the spreadsheet — usually at X requests/day the per-token cost crosses over.
[15:50] Luis Ortega: You keep saying X — can we get that number please?
[15:54] Alex Chen: We'll calculate exact numbers but expect the crossover in the low hundreds of thousands requests/day depending on the model. We'll put several sensitivity runs in the model (different cache hit rates, batching efficiencies).
[16:05] [18:00] Priya Nair: Also want to flag routing and fallback policies — Redwood can route high-priority fraud requests to dedicated low-latency pools and route analytics to cheaper pools; this hybrid approach often gives the best cost-latency balance.
[16:18] Maya Thompson: Are those routing rules managed in the console? Can we do per-route cost caps?
[16:23] Jordan Lee: Yes console supports per-route policies, fallbacks and quotas. You can set cost thresholds per-route and automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant if a threshold is hit.
[16:32] Hannah Park: Ok — finance would love that feature. Can we get a demo of the console controls?
[16:38] Alex Chen: Absolutely — we'll include a console demo as a follow-up.
[16:44] Derek Smith: Anything on observability retention costs? We need long traces tied to tokens.
[16:50] Priya Nair: We have token-level tracing and per-route dashboards. Long retention is an add-on — we'll provide pricing estimates but expect retention to scale with ingest.
[16:59] [20:00] Maya Thompson: Regarding security docs — can you send SOC2, penetration test summaries, and an example contract?
[20:08] Alex Chen: Yes — I'll send the security pack and the standard enterprise contract.
[20:12] Hannah Park: Great. On timeline — we'll need pilot results before Feb 28 to make a March decision. Is that workable?
[20:20] Priya Nair: Yes, a 4-week pilot starting early Feb can deliver results by end of Feb. We'll need the prompt set and volume forecast to start.
[20:30] Luis Ortega: One more technical — how do you handle KV cache invalidation for fraud models that require fresh user data?
[20:37] Jordan Lee: We support granular cache keys and TTLs, and programmatic invalidation via API. You can tie cache scopes to customer IDs or session IDs to avoid cross-tenant leakage.
[20:48] Maya Thompson: Ok that addresses my concern.
[20:52] [24:00] Hannah Park: Wrap up — what are the exact deliverables from Redwood in the next week?
[24:09] Alex Chen: We'll send: 1) cost model spreadsheet with sensitivity analysis, 2) security pack (SOC2, pen test summary, KMS integration docs), 3) benchmark runbook for pilot and a proposed timeline, 4) console demo invite.
[24:25] Priya Nair: And I'll include the initial sample prompt evaluation checklist and propose the three prompts for the benchmark.
[24:33] Maya Thompson: Perfect.
[24:36] Derek Smith: I'll coordinate network/VPC setup details with Alex after the call.
[24:41] Alex Chen: Great — thank you all. We'll follow up with the items.
[24:47] [End notes — transcription artifacts]: There were a few overlaps/crosstalks; some product names transcribed as Redwoods or Redwood Ded in places. References shared: cost model spreadsheet (link shared in chat), security pack (link), console demo calendar invite (sent).

Call length alignment note: The transcript captures high-level points and key timestamps; actual call had back-and-forth technical clarifications and a couple of long pauses while participants reviewed slides.
